title: Animal physiology
summary: How animal bodies work, compared across species.

layers.basics: Animals solve the same problems in different ways: getting energy and oxygen, moving fluids, balancing water and salts, controlling temperature and coordinating organs.
layers.deeper: Human organ systems are one example of a general plan; comparisons across fish, insects, birds and mammals show how physical constraints and evolution shape solutions.
layers.expert: Physiological scaling (Kleiber's law), countercurrent exchange and feedback control recur from kidneys to gills to heat exchangers, linking physiology to physics and evolution.

title: Animal form, size and scaling

layers.basics: Bigger animals have lower surface-area-to-volume ratios, so they lose less heat per gram and need special structures for exchange.
layers.deeper: Metabolic rate rises with mass, but less than proportionally: a shrew burns far more energy per gram than an elephant.
layers.expert: Kleiber's law: BMR ∝ M^0.75. The origin of the 3/4 exponent (fractal supply networks vs other models) is debated. Heart rate scales ≈ M^−0.25, so most mammals have ≈ 10⁹ lifetime heartbeats.

open_questions: The mechanistic origin and universality of the 3/4 exponent are still debated.

layers.basics: Animals get energy from food: carbohydrates, fats and proteins, and need vitamins, minerals and water.
layers.deeper: Basal metabolic rate is the minimum energy at rest. Ectotherms use ≈ 10× less energy than endotherms of the same size.
layers.expert: Respiratory quotient (CO₂/O₂) is ≈ 1.0 for carbohydrate, ≈ 0.7 for fat. Energy balance relates intake, work, heat and storage. Obesity and undernutrition are major public-health issues.

layers.basics: Animals have sac-like or tube-like guts. Herbivores have long guts or fermentation chambers, carnivores shorter ones.
layers.deeper: Ruminants (cows) ferment plant material in a rumen with microbes. Birds use a muscular gizzard with grit in place of teeth.
layers.expert: Hindgut fermenters (horses, rabbits) differ from foregut fermenters; microbial fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that supply ≈ 60–70% of a cow's energy.

title: Comparative circulation
summary: Open, closed, single and double circuits.

layers.basics: Insects have open circulation; fish have a single circuit with a two-chambered heart; birds and mammals have two circuits with a four-chambered heart.
layers.deeper: Double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate and allows high pressure systemic flow, supporting endothermy.
layers.expert: Amphibian and reptile three-chambered hearts allow shunting; crocodilians have a four-chambered heart with a foramen of Panizza. Blood pressure scales little with body size, except in giraffes (≈ 250 mmHg at heart level).

title: Gas exchange across animals

layers.basics: Small animals exchange gases through the skin. Fish use gills, insects use tracheal tubes and vertebrates on land use lungs.
layers.deeper: Fish gills use countercurrent flow to extract up to ≈ 80% of O₂ from water. Bird lungs have one-way airflow through air sacs, giving them an advantage at altitude.
layers.expert: Water holds ≈ 30× less O₂ than air and is 800× denser and ≈ 50× more viscous. Fick's law sets diffusion limits: rate ∝ area × ΔP / thickness.

facts: O₂ capacity of water vs air

layers.basics: Myoglobin stores oxygen in muscle. Diving mammals have high myoglobin, large blood volume and slow their heart rate.
layers.deeper: Elephant seals dive > 1 h; sperm whales over 2 h. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas with hemoglobin of high O₂ affinity.
layers.expert: Myoglobin has a hyperbolic binding curve with P₅₀ ≈ 2.8 mmHg, versus Hb ≈ 26 mmHg. Antarctic icefish have no hemoglobin at all, relying on dissolved O₂ in cold water.

layers.basics: Marine fish lose water and drink seawater; freshwater fish gain water and make dilute urine. Osmoconformers match their surroundings, osmoregulators do not.
layers.deeper: Salt glands, gills and kidneys excrete excess salts. Desert mammals make very concentrated urine.
layers.expert: Kangaroo rat urine reaches ≈ 5,000 mOsm/L (human max ≈ 1,200). Sharks retain urea and TMAO to equal seawater osmolarity (≈ 1,000 mOsm/L).

layers.basics: Flatworms use protonephridia, insects Malpighian tubules and vertebrates kidneys. Wastes are ammonia, urea or uric acid.
layers.deeper: Ammonia is toxic but water-hungry to excrete; uric acid is nearly dry. The choice reflects the habitat and egg-laying style.
layers.expert: The vertebrate nephron filters ≈ 180 L plasma per day, reabsorbing > 99%. Countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle builds the medullary gradient.

layers.basics: Endotherms (birds, mammals) make heat internally; ectotherms (most reptiles, fish, insects) rely on environmental heat and behaviour.
layers.deeper: Insulation, sweating, shivering, vasodilation and countercurrent heat exchange help control temperature. Hibernation and torpor save energy.
layers.expert: Endothermy costs ≈ 5–10× more energy but extends activity to cold and night. Bluefin tuna and some sharks are regionally endothermic using retia mirabilia. Brown fat uncoupling protein (UCP1) produces heat without ATP.

layers.basics: Animals support and move their bodies with hydrostatic skeletons (worms), exoskeletons (insects) or endoskeletons (vertebrates).
layers.deeper: Muscles work in antagonistic pairs across joints. Running, flying and swimming each have different mechanical trade-offs.
layers.expert: Cost of transport falls with body size and is lowest for swimming, then flying, then running. Insect flight muscles can be asynchronous, contracting multiple times per nerve impulse.

layers.basics: Hormones are chemical messengers released into the blood. Insects have ecdysone for moulting and juvenile hormone; vertebrates have a wide range of peptide and steroid hormones.
layers.deeper: Feedback keeps levels stable, such as thyroid hormone controlled via the hypothalamus and pituitary. Amphibian metamorphosis is driven by thyroid hormone.
layers.expert: Hormone classes: peptide, steroid, amine. Half-lives range from minutes (insulin ≈ 5 min) to days (thyroxine ≈ 7 days). The hypothalamic–pituitary axes work as cascades with negative feedback.

layers.basics: Animals reproduce sexually or asexually, with external or internal fertilisation, and lay eggs, give live birth or both.
layers.deeper: Parthenogenesis occurs in some insects, lizards and sharks. Hormones tightly control human cycles.
layers.expert: Reproductive strategies lie on an r/K continuum. Placental mammals nourish embryos via a placenta; marsupials give birth early; monotremes lay eggs.

title: Neuroscience and behavior
summary: How nervous systems sense, compute and drive behaviour.

layers.basics: Neurons send electrical and chemical signals. Networks of neurons sense the world, store memories, make decisions and control the body.
layers.deeper: Action potentials travel along axons, synapses pass the message, and plasticity changes connections with experience. Behaviour has both proximate (mechanism) and ultimate (evolutionary) explanations.
layers.expert: Understanding the brain spans scales: ion channels, synaptic plasticity, circuits and whole-brain dynamics. Many questions, such as consciousness and memory encoding, remain open.

layers.basics: Neurons have dendrites that receive input, a cell body and an axon that sends output. Glia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia) support them.
layers.deeper: Myelin from oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells speeds conduction. The brain has ≈ 86 billion neurons and about as many glia.
layers.expert: Neuron types are classified by shape, transmitter and gene expression (hundreds of types by single-cell RNA-seq). Axon lengths reach 1 m or more in humans.

layers.basics: When a neuron's membrane voltage reaches threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, causing a rapid spike that is then terminated by K⁺ channels.
layers.deeper: The spike regenerates down the axon without weakening. Refractory periods keep it moving in one direction.
layers.expert: Hodgkin and Huxley's squid axon model (1952) describes the gating variables m, h, n. Peak potential ≈ +30 to +40 mV; speed ≈ 1 m/s unmyelinated to ≈ 120 m/s myelinated (saltatory conduction).

layers.basics: At a synapse, an arriving spike triggers release of neurotransmitter, which binds receptors on the next cell and excites or inhibits it.
layers.deeper: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter and GABA the main inhibitory one. Others: dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine.
layers.expert: Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle fusion (SNAREs) within ≈ 0.2 ms. Ionotropic receptors act in ms; metabotropic ones in 100s ms to s. SSRIs block serotonin reuptake; botulinum toxin cleaves SNAREs.

title: Synaptic plasticity, learning and memory

layers.basics: Synapses strengthen or weaken with use. This is a main basis for learning and memory.
layers.deeper: Long-term potentiation (LTP) in the hippocampus is the best studied form. Memories move from short-term to long-term storage via consolidation.
layers.expert: LTP involves NMDA receptors, Ca²⁺ influx and AMPA receptor insertion. H.M. showed the hippocampus is needed to form new declarative memories. How engrams store information over years remains an active question.

open_questions: How long-term memory is physically encoded and maintained across molecular turnover is unresolved.

layers.basics: Receptors convert light, sound, chemicals, touch and heat into electrical signals. Different receptor types respond to different stimuli.
layers.deeper: Sensory neurons adapt to constant stimuli. Signal strength is coded by firing rate and number of cells.
layers.expert: Weber–Fechner and Stevens' power law relate stimulus to perceived intensity. TRP channels sense temperature and chemicals; Piezo channels sense force (2021 Nobel).

layers.basics: Light hits rods and cones in the retina. A pigment molecule changes shape and starts a signal that travels via the optic nerve to the brain.
layers.deeper: Rods work in dim light; cones give colour (three types in humans). The fovea has the sharpest vision.
layers.expert: Retinal isomerises from 11-cis to all-trans in ≈ 200 fs; the cascade (rhodopsin → transducin → PDE) amplifies a single photon response ≈ 10⁵-fold. Rods can respond to single photons.

layers.basics: Hair cells in the cochlea turn sound vibrations into signals. Taste and smell detect molecules with chemical receptors.
layers.deeper: Humans have ≈ 400 functional olfactory receptor genes and five basic tastes. The vestibular system senses head motion.
layers.expert: The cochlea performs a frequency analysis along the basilar membrane (≈ 20 Hz–20 kHz). Olfactory receptors are GPCRs; Buck and Axel won the 2004 Nobel.

title: Organisation of the central nervous system

layers.basics: The brain's major regions are the cerebrum (thinking, senses, movement), cerebellum (coordination) and brainstem (vital functions).
layers.deeper: The cerebral cortex has four lobes. Hippocampus is key for memory, amygdala for emotion and hypothalamus for homeostasis.
layers.expert: Brain mass ≈ 1.4 kg (2% of body mass, ≈ 20% of resting energy). Functional specialisation coexists with distributed networks; connectomics maps wiring (fly connectome 2023, ≈ 140,000 neurons).

layers.basics: The sympathetic system prepares the body for action ("fight or flight") and the parasympathetic system promotes rest and digestion.
layers.deeper: A reflex arc (sensor, spinal circuit, effector) gives fast responses without the brain, such as the knee jerk.
layers.expert: Sympathetic postganglionic fibres use noradrenaline and parasympathetic use acetylcholine. Baroreflex adjusts heart rate within 1–2 beats of blood-pressure change.

title: Sleep and circadian rhythms

layers.basics: Animals have internal clocks with a ≈ 24 h cycle set by light. Sleep alternates between NREM and REM stages.
layers.deeper: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the master clock; melatonin from the pineal rises at night.
layers.expert: Clock genes (PER, CRY, CLOCK, BMAL1) form a transcription–translation feedback loop with ≈ 24 h period (Nobel 2017). Sleep functions (memory, waste clearance) are active research topics.

open_questions: The core biological function of sleep is not settled.

title: Neurological disorders

layers.basics: Disorders include stroke, epilepsy, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and multiple sclerosis.
layers.deeper: Parkinson's disease follows loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra; MS is autoimmune demyelination.
layers.expert: Alzheimer's is linked to amyloid-β plaques and tau tangles; amyloid-targeting antibodies slow decline modestly. Causal chains and best targets remain contested.

open_questions: The causal role of amyloid and tau in Alzheimer's disease and best therapeutic targets are still debated.

title: Animal behaviour: proximate and ultimate causes

layers.basics: Behaviour has immediate causes (hormones, neurons) and evolutionary causes (why selection favoured it).
layers.deeper: Tinbergen asked: mechanism, development, function and evolution. Fixed action patterns (egg-rolling in geese) are innate; imprinting and song learning are learned.
layers.expert: Behavioural genetics (foraging gene in Drosophila) and optimality models link genes to ecology. Nobel to Lorenz, Tinbergen, von Frisch (1973).

title: Learning, foraging and social behaviour

layers.basics: Animals learn through habituation, conditioning and imitation. They also forage, defend territories, form groups and sometimes cooperate.
layers.deeper: Optimal foraging models predict diet choice. Honeybees communicate food location by the waggle dance (von Frisch).
layers.expert: Marginal value theorem predicts when to leave a patch. Eusocial insects and naked mole-rats have reproductive division of labour; cooperative breeding is common in birds.

facts: leave when rate drops to average

title: Migration and animal navigation

layers.basics: Birds, turtles, salmon and butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres using the Sun, stars, magnetic fields and smell.
layers.deeper: Arctic terns migrate ≈ 70,000 km a year. Salmon return to natal streams using odour cues.
layers.expert: Magnetoreception may involve cryptochromes (radical-pair mechanism) and magnetite. Evidence for specifics remains incomplete.

open_questions: The molecular basis of magnetoreception in animals is not established.

layers.basics: Neuroscientists record electrical activity (EEG, patch clamp), image the brain (fMRI, PET) and manipulate circuits with light (optogenetics).
layers.deeper: EEG has ms resolution but poor spatial detail; fMRI has mm resolution but is slow (seconds).
layers.expert: fMRI measures BOLD, an indirect proxy for neural activity. Two-photon calcium imaging records hundreds of neurons; Neuropixels probes record from thousands. Statistical issues in neuroimaging (cluster inflation, small samples) are known concerns.
